newsitem.title: UK: OPTIONS - May coffee vols slashed, cocoa stays firm.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - May coffee vols slashed, cocoa stays firm.

text.p: May coffee volatilies lost ground this week as locals shuffled positions to grab higher returns, but forward premiums were kept relatively firm against a frost scare in Brazil this summer.
Cocoa vols remained strong amid a string of orders on July calls with players positioning against a possible flare-up in buoyant futures.
"There is a big interest in July out-of-the-money calls and only few sellers," said one cocoa options market maker.
July vols traded at a steady 27 percent but looked set to climb higher in tandem with a new assault on recent highs signalled in futures charts.
The key May futures were trying to shake off their recent consolidative tone and pierce the nearby 1,037 to secure a hike towards 1,100.
Other active July call strikes were 1,100, 1,000 and 1,050.

Demand was also brewing for September calls but sellers were reluctant to take the plunge in case of a last minute squeeze or crop surprises. Last year, the September contract had spearheaded a rally to eight-year highs.
In coffee, a bout of local selling pushed May vols down to 42 percent after trading at 47-48 earlier this week but July strikes were firm.
"Generally it's just locals jobbing the vols around and forcing them down," said one trader.

The weakness also reflected the change of sentiment in futures where players expect the benchmark May to test the ominous $1,600. A breach of this level could knock it down to the February low of $1,460 if support fails at $1,550 and $1,500, traders and analysts said.
But in options, volatility traders were selling at-the-money May calls, mainly $1,700, and bidding them back at 39.5-40 percent whilst rolling strikes to $1,800.

Activity was also cited in May $1,700-$1,800 call spread and the May-July calender call spread which gave the player a brisk premium of up to five percent this week. The May/July spread widened from 2-3 pct last week.
"They are keeping the July vols pretty tight. They are not going to pay up too much yet because of the frost season," said one trader.
Another highlight of the week was a July $1,400-$1,900 strangle which involved buying the $1,400 put as well as the $1,900 call.
Some players dabbled in September options, particularly the $2,150 calls which were sold at a strong 70 pct.
"Even though it's the frost season it's quite an interesting punt," said one trader.
White sugar options were dormant with no trades reported this week.
